meaning: Give (to out-group/someone of equal or lower status)

exercises.example_sentence: 私は友達に誕生日のプレゼントをあげた。
exercises.translation: I gave my friend a birthday present.
wrong_choice_explanations: くれた describes giving TO the speaker's side; with 私は as the giver, a くれる form is impossible.
くださった is the respectful くれる, used when someone gives TO the speaker; here the speaker is the giver.
あがった is the intransitive 'went up'; it can't take プレゼントを as an object and doesn't mean 'give'.

exercises.example_sentence: 私は妹に手作りのクッキーをあげました。
exercises.translation: I gave homemade cookies to my younger sister.
wrong_choice_explanations: くれました would mean someone gave TO the speaker's side; with 私は as the giver, a くれる form is impossible.
さしあげました is the humble 'give' used toward people you must show respect to; it is not used for your own younger sister.
あがりました is the intransitive 'went up'; it can't take クッキーを as an object and doesn't mean 'give'.

exercises.example_sentence: 記念日に、恋人にバラの花をあげるつもりです。
exercises.translation: I intend to give my partner roses on our anniversary.
wrong_choice_explanations: つもり shows the speaker's own plan, so the speaker is the giver; くれる can only describe giving toward the speaker's side.
くださる is the respectful くれる, used when someone gives TO the speaker; it can't describe the speaker's own plan to give.
あがる is intransitive ('go up'); it can't take バラの花を as an object and doesn't mean 'give'.

audio_alternatives.hiragana_full: きねんびにはこいびとにばらをあげるつもりだ。

exercises.example_sentence: 息子に新しいゲームをあげよう。
exercises.translation: Let's give our son a new game.
wrong_choice_explanations: さしあげよう is the humble 'give' used toward people of higher status; parents don't use it toward their own son.
いただこう means humbly 'receive'; it reverses the direction (the parents are giving) and is far too humble toward one's own son.
あがろう is the intransitive 'let's go up'; it can't take ゲームを as an object and doesn't mean 'give'.

exercises.example_sentence: 犬に新しいおもちゃをあげた。
exercises.translation: I gave the dog a new toy.
wrong_choice_explanations: もらった would mean the toy was received FROM the dog, but a dog can't give anyone a toy; the toy went to the dog.
さしあげた is the humble 'give' used toward people of higher status; it is never used toward an animal.
あがった is the intransitive 'went up'; it can't take おもちゃを as an object and doesn't mean 'give'.

exercises.example_sentence: 私は祖父に旅行の写真をあげました。
exercises.translation: I gave my grandfather the photos from my trip.
wrong_choice_explanations: くれました describes giving TO the speaker's side; with 私は as the giver, a くれる form is impossible.
くださいました is the respectful くれる, for someone giving TO the speaker; here the speaker is the giver.
あがりました is the intransitive 'went up'; it can't take 写真を as an object and doesn't mean 'give'.

exercises.example_sentence: 私は近所の子供たちに絵本を読んであげました。
exercises.translation: I read picture books to the neighborhood children.
wrong_choice_explanations: 読んでくれました would mean someone read FOR the speaker's side; with 私は as the reader, a くれる form is impossible.
読んでさしあげました is the humble 'do for' used toward people of higher status; it is not used toward small children.
読んでくださいました is the respectful くれる, for someone doing something FOR the speaker; here the speaker is the one reading.

exercises.example_sentence: 同級生に辞書をあげたい。
exercises.translation: I want to give a dictionary to my classmate.
wrong_choice_explanations: たい shows the speaker's own wish, so the speaker is the giver; くれる only describes giving toward the speaker, so くれたい is impossible.
くださる is the respectful くれる (giving TO the speaker) and is never used with the speaker's own たい wish.
あがりたい is the intransitive 'want to go up'; it can't take 辞書を as an object and doesn't mean 'give'.

exercises.example_sentence: 私は後輩に仕事のやり方を教えてあげた。
exercises.translation: I taught my junior colleague how to do the job.
wrong_choice_explanations: てくれた means someone did something FOR the speaker's side; with 私は as the one teaching, it is impossible.
てさしあげた is the humble 'do for' used toward people above you; you don't use it toward a junior (後輩).
てくださった is the respectful てくれた, for someone doing something FOR the speaker; here the speaker is the one teaching.
